title.en: Section 1 - Telephone Conversation About Joining a Health Club
title.zh: 第一部分 - 关于加入健身俱乐部的电话对话

sections.passage:
A woman calls the Riverside Health Club to inquire about membership options. The receptionist, Paul, answers the phone and provides detailed information about the club's facilities and membership plans.

Paul explains that the club recently underwent a major renovation and now features a 25-meter heated swimming pool, a fully equipped gym with over 100 pieces of exercise equipment, three exercise studios for group classes, a sauna and steam room, and a juice bar. The club also has two outdoor tennis courts and a running track that circles the grounds.

The woman asks about the different membership options available. Paul describes three tiers: the standard membership at 50 pounds per month gives access to the gym and swimming pool during standard hours from 6 AM to 10 PM. The premium membership at 75 pounds per month includes all standard facilities plus access to the sauna and steam room, unlimited group fitness classes, and extended hours from 5 AM to midnight. The platinum membership at 100 pounds per month adds personal training sessions, priority court booking for tennis, and guest passes for up to two visitors per month.

The woman mentions she is a university student, and Paul tells her about the student discount of 20 percent off any membership tier, available with a valid student ID. There is also a one-time registration fee of 30 pounds for new members, though Paul mentions there is currently a promotional offer that waives this fee for anyone who signs up before the end of the month. The minimum contract period is six months, but members can freeze their membership for up to two months per year at no additional cost if they notify the club at least two weeks in advance.

text.zh: 女士为什么打电话给健身俱乐部？

title.en: Section 2 - Introduction to a Community Garden Project
title.zh: 第二部分 - 社区花园项目介绍

sections.passage:
Welcome, everyone, to the launch of our community garden project. My name is Linda Carter, and I'm the project coordinator for the Greenway Community Trust. Thank you all for coming today. I'm delighted to see so much interest in this initiative.

Our community garden is located on the corner of Oak Street and River Road, on a site that was previously an unused car park belonging to the old factory. The local council has granted us a ten-year lease on the land, and we've spent the last six months clearing the site, testing the soil, and installing water and electricity connections. The total area is approximately 2,000 square meters, which we've divided into several distinct zones.

The largest section, covering about 800 square meters, is divided into 50 individual allotment plots, each measuring 3 meters by 5 meters. These plots are available for individual members to grow their own fruit, vegetables, and flowers. Annual rental for a standard plot is 25 pounds, or 15 pounds for senior citizens and those receiving benefits. We also have ten raised beds specifically designed for wheelchair users and people with mobility difficulties.

In addition to the allotment plots, we have created a communal herb garden that is freely available to all community members, a children's growing area where local schools can bring students for educational visits, a wildlife pond and nature trail, and a covered pavilion with seating for up to 40 people. The pavilion includes basic kitchen facilities and can be hired for community events at a cost of 50 pounds per half day.

We run a weekly gardening workshop every Saturday morning from 10 AM to noon, covering topics such as composting, organic pest control, seed saving, and seasonal planting. These workshops are free for garden members and 5 pounds per session for non-members. We also host a monthly community meal on the last Sunday of each month, where we cook dishes using produce grown in the garden. Our next meal is scheduled for March 28th, and everyone is welcome.

title.en: Section 3 - Tutorial Discussion on an Environmental Science Assignment
title.zh: 第三部分 - 关于环境科学作业的辅导讨论

sections.passage:
Two students, Emma and Jake, are meeting with their tutor, Dr. Patel, to discuss their upcoming assignment on water management strategies in developing countries. The assignment requires them to compare two different approaches and present their findings in a 3,000-word report.

Dr. Patel begins by asking about their chosen focus. Emma explains that they have decided to compare rainwater harvesting systems in rural India with desalination technology in the Middle East. She believes this comparison is interesting because the two approaches represent fundamentally different solutions to the same problem of water scarcity, one working with natural water sources and the other creating new sources through technology.

Jake adds that their preliminary research has revealed some fascinating data. In India, traditional rainwater harvesting has been practiced for thousands of years, but many ancient systems have fallen into disrepair. A government initiative launched in 2015 has funded the restoration of over 10,000 traditional systems and the construction of 5,000 new ones across Rajasthan and Tamil Nadu. These systems can collect and store up to 100,000 liters of water during the monsoon season, providing sufficient water for approximately 50 families for up to six months.

Regarding desalination, Jake explains that the technology has become increasingly efficient but remains expensive. The largest desalination plant in the world, located in Ras Al Khair in Saudi Arabia, produces over one million cubic meters of fresh water per day. However, the energy costs are enormous, and the process generates highly concentrated brine waste that can damage marine ecosystems when discharged into the sea.

Dr. Patel encourages them to consider the sustainability implications of both approaches. She suggests they examine the carbon footprint of each method, the long-term maintenance requirements, and the potential for community ownership and management. She also recommends they include a cost-benefit analysis comparing the two systems over a 20-year period, taking into account not just financial costs but also social and environmental factors.

title.en: Section 4 - Lecture on the History of Chocolate
title.zh: 第四部分 - 关于巧克力历史的讲座

sections.passage:
Good afternoon, everyone. Today I'll be tracing the fascinating history of chocolate, from its origins as a bitter ceremonial drink in ancient Mesoamerica to the sweet confection we know today. This is a story that spans over 3,000 years and involves exploration, colonialism, scientific innovation, and industrial revolution.

The story of chocolate begins with the cacao tree, Theobroma cacao, which is native to the tropical regions of Central and South America. The word Theobroma literally means 'food of the gods' in Greek, reflecting the reverence in which cacao was held by ancient civilizations. Archaeological evidence suggests that the Olmec people of southern Mexico were the first to cultivate cacao and process its beans into a drink, as early as 1500 BC. The Maya and Aztec civilizations later adopted and refined these practices, creating elaborate preparation rituals for what they called xocolatl, meaning 'bitter water.'

For the Aztecs, cacao was a luxury item of immense cultural and economic significance. It was used as currency, with a single turkey costing about 100 cacao beans, and a rabbit about 30 beans. The emperor Montezuma II was reported to drink up to 50 cups of xocolatl per day, served in golden goblets. The drink was typically flavored with vanilla, chili peppers, and achiote, and was quite different from modern hot chocolate. It was served cold, often frothy, and was extremely bitter by today's standards.

Chocolate arrived in Europe in the early 16th century following the Spanish conquest of the Aztec Empire. The Spanish explorer Hernan Cortes is widely credited with introducing cacao to the Spanish court, though it was initially met with skepticism due to its unfamiliar taste. The Spanish began adding sugar and cinnamon to make it more palatable to European tastes, and by the late 16th century, chocolate drinking had become fashionable among the Spanish aristocracy. Over the following century, the trend spread to France, Italy, and eventually England, where the first chocolate house opened in London in 1657.

The industrialization of chocolate production in the 19th century transformed it from an expensive luxury into an affordable treat for the masses. In 1828, Dutch chemist Coenraad van Houten invented a hydraulic press that could extract cocoa butter from roasted cacao beans, leaving behind a dry powder that could be mixed with water to create a smoother drink. This process, known as 'Dutching,' also reduced the bitterness of the chocolate. More significantly, the separation of cocoa butter enabled the creation of solid chocolate. In 1847, the British company J.S. Fry and Sons produced the first modern chocolate bar by combining cocoa powder, sugar, and melted cocoa butter.

The Swiss made further breakthroughs in chocolate production. In 1875, Daniel Peter added condensed milk to chocolate to create milk chocolate. Three years later, his neighbor Henri Nestle helped him establish a company to mass-produce the product. Meanwhile, Rodolphe Lindt developed the conching machine in 1879, a device that agitated chocolate for hours or even days to produce a smoother, more refined texture. These innovations laid the foundation for the modern chocolate industry, which is now worth over 130 billion dollars globally and employs an estimated 50 million people along its supply chain.

text.zh: 'Theobroma'在希腊语中是什么意思？

title.zh: 文章1 - 让我们了解蝙蝠

sections.passage:
Bats have a problem: how to find their way around in the dark. They hunt at night, and cannot use light to help them find prey and avoid obstacles. You might say that this is a problem of their own making, one that they could avoid simply by changing their habits and hunting by day. But the daytime economy is already heavily exploited by other creatures such as birds. Given that there is a choice, it is better to use a sense that works at night than to use one that works during the day and not at night. So bats have evolved a system of sonar, using sound rather than light, to navigate and hunt in complete darkness.

This system, known as echolocation, was first described by the Italian biologist Lazzaro Spallanzani in the 18th century. Spallanzani conducted a series of experiments in which he showed that bats could navigate perfectly well even when he blinded them, but became disoriented when he blocked their ears. He concluded that bats used their hearing to orient themselves, though he was unable to explain exactly how the system worked. It was not until the development of ultrasonic detection equipment in the early 20th century that scientists were able to confirm that bats emit high-frequency sound waves and use the returning echoes to build a detailed picture of their surroundings.

Modern research has revealed that echolocation is an extraordinarily sophisticated system. A hunting bat can emit up to 200 ultrasonic pulses per second and process the returning echoes in real time to detect and track insects in flight. Some species can detect objects as thin as a human hair and can distinguish between different types of insects based on the characteristics of the returning echo. The accuracy of bat echolocation is remarkable: bats can detect and catch prey in complete darkness, navigate through complex environments at high speed, and even detect water surfaces by recognizing the unique acoustic signature of a flat, reflective surface.

The principles of bat echolocation have inspired numerous human technologies. Sonar, the underwater detection system used by submarines and ships, was directly inspired by research into bat navigation. Radar, used for aircraft detection and air traffic control, operates on similar principles, though it uses radio waves rather than sound. More recently, engineers have developed ultrasonic navigation aids for blind and visually impaired people that work on echolocation principles. Researchers at the University of Bristol have created a handheld device that emits ultrasonic pulses and translates the returning echoes into tactile feedback, enabling users to detect obstacles and navigate unfamiliar environments.

Despite their remarkable abilities, bats face increasing threats from human activity. Habitat destruction, pesticide use, and climate change are all contributing to declining bat populations worldwide. In the UK alone, bat populations have declined by an estimated 70 percent since the 1970s. All British bat species are now legally protected, and it is an offense to deliberately kill, injure, or disturb bats or to damage their roosting sites. Conservation efforts include the installation of bat boxes in parks and gardens, the preservation of hedgerows and woodland corridors, and the creation of wildlife-friendly farming practices that reduce pesticide use and maintain insect populations on which bats depend.

title.en: Passage 2 - The True Cost of Food
title.zh: 文章2 - 食品的真实成本

sections.passage:
A growing number of economists, environmentalists, and food policy experts argue that the price we pay for food in shops does not reflect its true cost. When we factor in the environmental damage caused by modern agriculture, the health costs of diet-related diseases, and the subsidies paid to farmers by taxpayers, the real price of food is significantly higher than what appears on the supermarket shelf. This concept, known as the 'true cost' of food, has profound implications for how we produce, distribute, and consume food.

Environmental costs represent perhaps the largest hidden component of food prices. Modern industrial agriculture relies heavily on chemical fertilizers and pesticides, which contaminate waterways, degrade soil quality, and reduce biodiversity. A study by the UK's Environment Agency estimated that agricultural pollution costs the British economy approximately 1.5 billion pounds per year in water treatment and environmental remediation. Additionally, food production accounts for approximately 26 percent of global greenhouse gas emissions, with livestock farming alone responsible for about 14.5 percent. These climate costs are externalized, meaning they are not reflected in the price consumers pay for food.

Health costs represent another significant hidden expense. The World Health Organization estimates that poor diet contributes to approximately 11 million deaths annually worldwide, making it a bigger killer than tobacco. In the UK, the National Health Service spends an estimated 6.1 billion pounds per year treating obesity-related conditions, and a further 2.3 billion pounds on treating type 2 diabetes. Many of these conditions are directly linked to the overconsumption of cheap, processed foods that are high in sugar, salt, and saturated fat. If the health costs of unhealthy food were included in its price, a typical fast-food meal would cost significantly more.

Agricultural subsidies further distort food prices. In the European Union, the Common Agricultural Policy distributes approximately 58 billion euros per year to farmers, with the majority going to large-scale producers of staple crops such as wheat, corn, and sugar. Critics argue that these subsidies encourage overproduction, depress global food prices, and disadvantage farmers in developing countries who cannot compete with subsidized European exports. In the United States, farm subsidies total approximately 20 billion dollars per year, with similar patterns of distribution favoring large agribusiness corporations over small family farms.

Several countries are beginning to experiment with policies that account for the true cost of food. Denmark has introduced a tax on saturated fat, and Mexico has imposed a levy on sugary drinks. In the UK, the government's National Food Strategy, published in 2021, recommended a sugar and salt reformulation tax, the expansion of free school meals, and the introduction of mandatory reporting of food waste by large food companies. These measures aim to shift the burden of food's hidden costs from society at large back onto the producers and consumers of unhealthy and unsustainable food products.

However, implementing true-cost food pricing raises serious concerns about social equity. Higher food prices would disproportionately affect low-income households, for whom food already represents a much larger share of total spending. Any policy reform must therefore include measures to protect vulnerable populations, such as increased welfare payments, subsidized healthy food programs, and improved access to affordable fresh produce in underserved communities. The challenge is to create a food system that accurately reflects costs while ensuring that nutritious food remains accessible to all.

sections.passage:
Educating Psyche by Bernie Neville is a book which looks at radical new approaches to learning, discussing the impact of emotions, imagination, and the unconscious on the learning process. The book draws on a wide range of research in psychology and neuroscience to argue that traditional educational methods, which emphasize rational thought and logical analysis, fail to engage the full spectrum of human cognitive abilities.

One of the central ideas in the book is that learning is not simply an intellectual activity but an holistic experience involving the whole person. Neville argues that effective learning requires the engagement of what he calls the 'four dimensions' of human experience: the somatic dimension (the body and physical sensations), the cognitive dimension (thought and analysis), the affective dimension (emotions and feelings), and the imaginal dimension (images, dreams, and fantasies). Traditional education, he suggests, focuses almost exclusively on the cognitive dimension while neglecting the other three.

The concept of 'suggestopedia,' developed by the Bulgarian psychiatrist Georgi Lozanov, is one of the approaches Neville examines in detail. Suggestopedia is based on the principle that learning can be dramatically accelerated when the learner is in a state of deep relaxation. In a typical suggestopedic lesson, students recline in comfortable chairs while listening to baroque music. The teacher reads the learning material in a specific rhythm, varying the tone and volume of their voice. Students are encouraged to let the material wash over them without making a conscious effort to memorize it. Lozanov claimed that this method could enable students to learn a foreign language in just one month, compared to the several years typically required.

While Lozanov's claims have been difficult to verify independently, research into the role of the unconscious in learning has produced some compelling findings. Studies at the University of California found that students who were exposed to information while sleeping showed improved recall of that information the following day, suggesting that the brain continues to process and consolidate learning during sleep. Similarly, research on 'incidental learning' has shown that people absorb information more effectively when they are not consciously trying to learn, which supports the idea that conscious effort can sometimes interfere with the learning process.

Neville also discusses the role of imagination in learning, arguing that the ability to form vivid mental images is a powerful tool for understanding and retaining information. Research has consistently shown that students who visualize concepts and create mental stories about what they are learning outperform those who rely on rote memorization and repetition. The technique of creating a 'memory palace,' in which information is associated with specific locations in an imagined physical space, dates back to ancient Greek orators and has been shown to be remarkably effective in modern experimental studies.

The practical implications of these ideas are significant. If Neville and the researchers he draws on are correct, then the traditional classroom environment may be fundamentally at odds with how the brain naturally learns. Rearranging classrooms to include comfortable seating, background music, and opportunities for movement and creative expression could, according to this view, lead to dramatic improvements in learning outcomes. Some progressive schools have already begun experimenting with these ideas, creating learning environments that are designed to engage all four of Neville's dimensions of human experience.

text.en: What type of music is used in suggestopedic lessons?
text.zh: 暗示教学法课程使用什么类型的音乐？

text.en: How long did Lozanov claim his method could teach a foreign language?
text.zh: Lozanov声称他的方法能在多长时间内教会一门外语？

text.en: What did research at the University of California find about sleeping and learning?
text.zh: 加利福尼亚大学关于睡眠和学习的研究发现了什么？

options.en: Sleep has no effect on learning
Sleeping before studying is most effective
The brain continues to process information during sleep
options.zh: 大脑在睡眠期间继续处理信息

options.en: Students should study immediately before sleeping
options.zh: 学生应该在睡前立即学习

text.en: What does research on incidental learning suggest?
text.zh: 关于附带学习的研究表明了什么？

options.zh: 有意识的努力总是改善学习

options.en: People absorb information better when not consciously trying to learn
options.zh: 人们在不刻意学习时吸收信息更好

options.en: Memorization is the best learning strategy
options.zh: 记忆是最好的学习策略
背景噪音有助于集中注意力

text.en: What is a 'memory palace'?
text.zh: 什么是'记忆宫殿'？

options.en: A technique associating information with locations in an imagined space
options.zh: 一种将信息与想象空间中的位置相关联的技术

text.en: When does the memory palace technique date back to?
text.zh: 记忆宫殿技术可以追溯到什么时候？

text.en: According to Neville, what may the traditional classroom be at odds with?
text.zh: 根据Neville的观点，传统教室可能与什么相矛盾？

text.en: Which dimension do traditional education methods primarily focus on?
text.zh: 传统教育方法主要关注哪个维度？

text.en: What do students who visualize concepts outperform?
text.zh: 将概念形象化的学生会超越哪些人？

options.en: Students who rely on rote memorization

text.en: What does Neville argue effective learning requires?
text.zh: Neville认为有效的学习需要什么？

options.en: Engagement of all four dimensions of human experience
options.zh: 人类体验四个维度的参与

prompt.en: The table below gives information about changes in modes of travel in England between 1985 and 2000. Summarize the information by selecting and reporting the main features, and make comparisons where relevant. Write at least 150 words.
prompt.zh: 下面的表格提供了1985年至2000年间英格兰出行方式变化的信息。通过选择和报告主要特征来总结信息，并在相关处进行比较。至少写150个单词。

prompt.en: It is generally believed that some people are born with certain talents, for instance for sport or music, and others are not. However, it is sometimes claimed that any child can be taught to become a good sports person or musician. Discuss both these views and give your own opinion. Write at least 250 words.
prompt.zh: 人们普遍认为有些人生来就具有某些天赋，比如体育或音乐方面，而有些人则没有。然而，有时有人声称任何孩子都可以被教导成为优秀的运动员或音乐家。讨论这两种观点并给出你自己的看法。至少写250个单词。
